title: tcpdump
description: The classic command-line packet capture and filtering tool built on libpcap, using Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax. Simpler and more universally available than tshark for quick captures and scripting.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
Current stable is **tcpdump 4.99.6** (Dec 2025), paired with **libpcap 1.10.x**; a 5.0 release has been in progress but not yet shipped as of late 2026.

tcpdump is a *packet sniffer*: it asks the kernel for a copy of raw network frames on an interface (via libpcap) and prints or saves them. It needs elevated access because reading raw traffic off a network card is a privileged operation on every OS.

## 1. Install

```bash
# Arch
sudo pacman -S tcpdump

# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install tcpdump

# Fedora
sudo dnf install tcpdump
```

Verify it installed and check the version:

```bash
tcpdump --version
```

## 2. Run without full root, via capabilities

```bash
sudo setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin=eip $(command -v tcpdump)
```

After this, your normal user can capture without `sudo` (though writing to some system paths may still need it). Verify with:

```bash
getcap $(command -v tcpdump)
```

To undo it later: `sudo setcap -r $(command -v tcpdump)`.

## 3. List interfaces

Before capturing, see what's actually available to listen on:

```bash
tcpdump -D
```

This prints every interface libpcap can see (e.g. `eth0`, `wlan0`, `lo`, `any`, `docker0`), numbered. `any` is a pseudo-interface that captures on all of them at once (Linux only), useful when you don't know which one carries the traffic you want.

## 4. First capture

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i wlan0 -c 10
```

`-i` picks the interface, `-c 10` stops after 10 packets so you're not staring at a scrolling terminal. Each line is a one-line summary: timestamp, source, destination, and a protocol summary. See [BPF Filters](/tcpdump/bpf-filters/) for narrowing this down to just the traffic you care about.

## 5. Quit safely

A live, unbounded capture (no `-c`) runs until you press `Ctrl+C`. tcpdump prints a packet-count summary on exit (`N packets captured`, `N packets received by filter`, `N packets dropped by kernel`) — the last two numbers matter: a gap between them means the kernel couldn't keep up and silently dropped packets, usually under heavy traffic with a slow filter or slow disk.
Getting Started.BPF Filters:
tcpdump filters use Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) syntax — the same language tshark's `-f` capture filter accepts, and worth learning once since it transfers directly. The filter, if given, is the last (non-flag) argument on the command line.

## Primitives

| Primitive | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `host` | `host 10.0.0.5` | Traffic to or from that address (works for IPv4, IPv6, or a hostname) |
| `net` | `net 10.0.0.0/24` | Traffic to or from any address in that subnet |
| `port` | `port 443` | Traffic on that port, either direction, TCP or UDP |
| `portrange` | `portrange 8000-8010` | Traffic on any port in that range |
| `src` / `dst` | `src host 10.0.0.5` | Restrict a primitive to one direction only |
| `tcp` / `udp` / `icmp` / `icmp6` | `tcp and port 22` | Restrict to a protocol |
| `arp` / `rarp` | `arp` | ARP/RARP frames |
| `ip` / `ip6` | `ip6` | Only IPv4 / only IPv6 |
| `ether host` | `ether host aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff` | Match by MAC address |
| `vlan` | `vlan 100` | Match 802.1Q-tagged frames (optionally a specific VLAN ID) |
| `broadcast` / `multicast` | `ip broadcast` | Broadcast/multicast frames |
| `less` / `greater` | `less 128` | Frame length comparison (bytes) |
| `gateway` | `gateway host1` | Packets that used host1 as a gateway (Ethernet source/dest differs from IP source/dest) |

## Direction qualifier

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'dst port 443'
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -Q in 'tcp'
```

`src`/`dst` restrict *addresses*; `-Q in|out|inout` (or the older `-Q` alias `-P`) restricts by which direction the packet traveled over that interface, useful for telling upload from download at a glance.

## Combining with logic

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp and (port 80 or port 443) and not src host 10.0.0.1'
```

`and`, `or`, `not` (or `&&`, `||`, `!`) compose primitives, evaluated left to right with `not` binding tightest and `and` before `or` — parenthesize instead of memorizing precedence. Quote the whole expression so the shell doesn't interpret the parentheses or `!`.

## TCP flags

```bash
sudo tcpdump 'tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0'
sudo tcpdump 'tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn'
```

Named flag constants: `tcp-syn`, `tcp-ack`, `tcp-fin`, `tcp-rst`, `tcp-push`, `tcp-urg`. The first form matches any packet with the SYN bit set (e.g. connection attempts, including SYN+ACK); the second matches a *bare* SYN with no other flags — the pattern for a fresh outbound connection request, handy for counting new connections without libraries like conntrack.

## Byte-offset matching

```bash
sudo tcpdump 'ip[0] & 0xf == 5'
```

`proto[offset]` (and `proto[offset:size]` for multi-byte fields) lets you reach into any header at an arbitrary byte and mask it — an escape hatch for anything without a named primitive. Rarely needed day to day, but it's why BPF can express almost any packet shape.

## A note on cost

Every primitive you add narrows what the kernel hands to tcpdump *before* it reaches userspace (the filter is compiled to BPF bytecode and run in-kernel), so a tight filter is cheaper than a loose one plus `grep` — filter first, don't just dump everything and pipe it through text tools.
Getting Started.Reading And Writing Captures:
## Write to a file

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap 'port 443'
```

`-w` writes raw packets in **pcap** format (not human-readable text, and not the newer **pcapng** format) — this is what tshark and Wireshark both read natively. Nothing is printed to the terminal while writing to a file unless you also add `-v`.

## Read back later

```bash
tcpdump -r capture.pcap -n
```

`-r` reads packets from a file instead of a live interface — no `sudo` needed, since you're not touching the network card. `-n` disables DNS/hostname resolution, which both speeds up reading and avoids the noise of resolver lookups changing output between runs (add `-nn` to also stop resolving port numbers to service names, e.g. `443` instead of `https`).

## Buffering: -l and -U

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -l 'port 53' | tee dns.log
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w - -U 'port 53' | ssh host 'cat > remote.pcap'
```

By default stdout is block-buffered when piped, so output to `grep`/`tee`/`awk` can lag. `-l` line-buffers text output for real-time piping. `-U` does the equivalent for `-w` output — it flushes each packet to the file/pipe as captured instead of batching, which matters when you're streaming a live `-w -` capture over a pipe (e.g. to `ssh` or `nc`) and want the far end to see packets promptly rather than in bursts.

## Snapshot length: how much of each packet is kept

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -s 0 -w full.pcap
```

`-s <bytes>` caps how many bytes of each packet are captured; `-s 0` (the modern default) captures the whole packet. A smaller snaplen (e.g. `-s 96`, old scripts often hardcode this) captures only headers and is faster/smaller when you don't need payload — but truncated packets can't be fully re-dissected later, so prefer `-s 0` unless you have a specific reason to trim.

## Splitting large captures: -C and -W

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w cap.pcap -C 100 -W 10
```

`-C 100` rotates to a new file every 100 MB; `-W 10` caps it at 10 files total, wrapping over the oldest. See [Rotating Captures](/tcpdump/rotating-captures/) for the time-based variant and combining both.

## Timestamp formats when reading/printing

| Flag | Format |
| --- | --- |
| (none) | Time of day, `HH:MM:SS.ffffff` |
| `-tt` | Unix epoch seconds |
| `-ttt` | Delta from previous printed packet |
| `-tttt` | Full date + time of day |
| `-ttttt` | Delta from first packet in the capture |

```bash
tcpdump -r capture.pcap -tttt -n
```

`-tttt` is the most useful for correlating a capture against logs from another system, since it includes the full date.

## Verbosity levels

| Flag | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| (none) | One-line summary |
| `-v` | + TTL, ID, total length, checksum |
| `-vv` | + more protocol-specific detail |
| `-vvv` | + full detail (e.g. complete NFS packet contents) |
| `-x` | Hex dump of packet (excluding link-level header) |
| `-X` | Hex + ASCII dump |
| `-A` | Print packet payload as ASCII only |
| `-e` | Print the link-level (Ethernet) header on every line |

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A 'tcp port 80'
```

Good for a quick eyeball of unencrypted HTTP traffic without a full protocol dissector. For encrypted traffic (TLS, SSH) the payload will just look like noise — `-A`/`-X` only help with plaintext protocols.
Getting Started.Interfaces And Privileges:
## Why root/capabilities are needed

Reading raw frames off a NIC bypasses the normal socket API, so the kernel gates it behind a privilege check: `CAP_NET_RAW` (to read packets) and `CAP_NET_ADMIN` (to set promiscuous/monitor mode). `sudo` grants both; the `setcap` approach from [Getting Started](/tcpdump/getting-started/) grants just those two to the tcpdump binary itself, which is the least-privilege option for a machine you use interactively.

## Promiscuous mode

By default tcpdump puts the interface into **promiscuous mode**, meaning the NIC hands up every frame it sees on the wire, not just ones addressed to this host — essential on a hub or a mirrored switch port, irrelevant on modern switched networks where you generally only receive your own traffic anyway (see below).

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -p
```

`-p` disables promiscuous mode. Use it when you deliberately want to see only traffic addressed to this host, or when changing the interface's promiscuous flag isn't allowed (some virtualized/cloud NICs reject it).

## Why you might not see other hosts' traffic

On a modern switched network, a switch only forwards a frame out the port the destination lives on — promiscuous mode doesn't help because the traffic never reaches your cable at all. To see traffic between *other* two hosts you need a SPAN/mirror port configured on the switch, or to be capturing on the router/gateway itself.

## Capturing on `any`

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i any -n
```

`any` (Linux-only) captures on every interface simultaneously, tagging each packet with which interface it arrived on. Convenient when you don't know which interface carries the traffic, but it can't put every interface into promiscuous mode and adds a small pseudo-header, so prefer naming a real interface once you know which one you need.

## Monitor mode (Wi-Fi)

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i wlan0 -I -y IEEE802_11_RADIO
```

`-I` puts a wireless interface into monitor mode, capturing raw 802.11 frames (including ones not addressed to this host) instead of the usual Ethernet-like view. `-y` picks the link-layer header type to use; `-L` lists which ones an interface supports. This is the same underlying mode `aircrack-ng`'s capture tools use — see the [aircrack-ng docs](/aircrack-ng/) if that's the goal, since `airmon-ng`/`airodump-ng` wrap this more conveniently for Wi-Fi work specifically.

Guides.Rotating Captures:
For always-on captures on a storage-constrained box, tcpdump has its own rotation flags — no external `logrotate` needed.

## Time-based rotation

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w '/var/log/pcap/cap-%Y%m%d-%H%M%S.pcap' \
  -G 3600 -W 24
```

`-G 3600` starts a new file every hour; `-W 24` keeps at most 24 files (one day), deleting the oldest as new ones are created. The `%Y%m%d-%H%M%S` in `-w` is a strftime pattern, substituted per file.

## Size-based rotation

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /var/log/pcap/cap.pcap -C 100 -W 10
```

`-C 100` rotates every 100 MB instead of by time; combine `-C` with `-G` to rotate on whichever limit hits first.

## Running a command after each file closes

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w '/var/log/pcap/cap-%s.pcap' -G 3600 -W 24 \
  -z /usr/local/bin/compress-pcap.sh
```

`-z <cmd>` runs `cmd <savefile>` once each rotated file is closed (not on the currently-open one) — a common use is compressing or shipping finished files off-box, e.g. a small script running `gzip "$1"`. Pair with `-Z <user>` (below) so the post-processing command doesn't run as root.

## Dropping privileges after opening the capture

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /var/log/pcap/cap.pcap -Z pcapuser
```

tcpdump needs root/capabilities only to *open* the raw socket; `-Z <user>` tells it to switch to that unprivileged user immediately afterward for the rest of its run (including any `-z` post-rotate command), limiting the blast radius if tcpdump itself were ever compromised while parsing untrusted traffic.

*Part of the [BPF Filters](/tcpdump/bpf-filters/) page.* Quick script to watch outbound DNS queries only.

Source: `example/watch_dns.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

IFACE="${1:-eth0}"

sudo tcpdump -i "$IFACE" -n -l 'udp port 53' \
  | grep --line-buffered 'A?'
```

Run it:

```bash
chmod +x example/watch_dns.sh
./example/watch_dns.sh wlan0
```
Guides.Filtering And Output Recipes:
Practical one-liners that combine filters, verbosity, and output flags for common troubleshooting tasks.

## Watch only new outbound TCP connections

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n 'tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn and src host 10.0.0.7'
```

Bare SYN (not SYN-ACK) from your own host is the signature of "we are opening a connection to somewhere" — useful for spotting an app phoning home to an unexpected address.

## Watch DNS queries and responses

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n -s 0 'udp port 53'
```

`-s 0` matters here: DNS responses (especially DNSSEC/large TXT records) can exceed the old default snaplen and get silently truncated in the printed output.

## Spot a SYN flood

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n 'tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn' | pv -l -i 5 > /dev/null
```

Count bare-SYN packets per interval; a sustained, abnormally high rate with many distinct source addresses (or one address, if unspoofed) is the classic SYN-flood signature. (`pv -l` here just counts lines per second — swap in `wc -l` over a fixed `-c` count if `pv` isn't installed.)

## Look at HTTP requests in cleartext

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -A -s 0 'tcp port 80 and (tcp[((tcp[12:1] & 0xf0) >> 2):4] = 0x47455420)'
```

That byte-offset expression matches a payload starting with `GET ` — a classic (if fiddly) BPF trick for filtering on the start of a TCP payload without a full protocol dissector. In practice, for anything past occasional debugging, [tshark](/tshark/) with a display filter (`http.request`) is far more readable — tcpdump's strength is capture, not deep inspection.

## Feed live traffic straight to Wireshark

```bash
ssh user@remote-host 'sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w - -U "port 443"' | wireshark -k -i -
```

`-w -` writes pcap to stdout instead of a file; piped over `ssh` and into Wireshark's `-i -` (read from stdin), this gives a live Wireshark view of a remote box's traffic without ever installing Wireshark there. `-U` (unbuffered) keeps packets flowing promptly instead of arriving in laggy bursts.

CLI Reference.tcpdump:
## Synopsis

```
tcpdump [options] [expression]
```

`expression` is a BPF filter (see [BPF Filters](/tcpdump/bpf-filters/)); when omitted, every packet on the interface is captured.

## Capture control

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-i <iface>` | Interface to capture on; `any` for all (Linux) |
| `-D`, `--list-interfaces` | List available capture interfaces and exit |
| `-c <n>` | Stop after `n` packets |
| `-p` | Don't put the interface into promiscuous mode |
| `-I` | Put a wireless interface into monitor mode |
| `-s <bytes>` | Snapshot length (bytes captured per packet); `0` = full packet |
| `-B <KB>`, `--buffer-size` | Kernel capture buffer size in KiB |
| `-y <type>`, `--linktype` | Set the link-layer header type to use |
| `-L`, `--list-data-link-types` | List link-layer types the interface supports and exit |
| `-j <type>`, `--time-stamp-type` | Set the timestamp type used by the capture |
| `-J`, `--list-time-stamp-types` | List timestamp types the interface supports |
| `-Q <dir>`, `-P <dir>` | Only capture packets going `in`, `out`, or `inout` |
| `--immediate-mode` | Deliver packets to the app as soon as they arrive, skipping buffering |

## Output: printing

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-n` | Disable hostname resolution |
| `-nn` | Disable hostname *and* port/service-name resolution |
| `-N` | Don't print domain qualification of hostnames |
| `-t` / `-tt` / `-ttt` / `-tttt` / `-ttttt` | Timestamp format (see [Reading And Writing Captures](/tcpdump/reading-and-writing-captures/)) |
| `-v`, `-vv`, `-vvv` | Increasing verbosity |
| `-q` | Quiet: less protocol detail per line |
| `-e` | Print link-level (Ethernet) header |
| `-x` / `-X` | Hex / hex+ASCII dump of packet payload |
| `-A` | Print packet payload as ASCII only |
| `-S` | Print absolute TCP sequence numbers instead of relative |
| `-#`, `--number` | Prefix each line with a packet number |
| `-K` | Don't verify checksums (needed when the NIC does checksum offload) |
| `-u` | Print undecoded NFS handles |
| `-l` | Line-buffer stdout (for piping to `grep`, `tee`, etc.) |
| `-U` | Packet-buffered: flush `-w` output after each packet |

## Files

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-w <file>` | Write raw packets to a file (`-` for stdout) |
| `-r <file>` | Read packets from a file (`-` for stdin) instead of live capture |
| `-F <file>` | Read the filter expression from a file instead of the command line |
| `-C <MB>` | Rotate `-w` output file every `MB` megabytes |
| `-G <sec>` | Rotate `-w` output file every `sec` seconds (use with a strftime pattern in `-w`) |
| `-W <n>` | Keep at most `n` rotated files |
| `-z <cmd>` | Run `cmd <savefile>` after each rotated file closes |
| `-Z <user>` | Drop root privileges to `<user>` after opening the capture |

## Filter/decode tuning

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-O` | Disable the BPF filter optimizer (debugging only) |
| `-d` / `-dd` / `-ddd` | Print the compiled BPF program (human-readable / C / decimal) and exit, without capturing |
| `-M <secret>` | Secret for validating TCP-MD5 protected segments |
| `-E <spi@addr algo:secret>` | Decrypt IPsec ESP packets using the given key |
| `-m <file>` | Load SMI MIB module definitions (for SNMP decoding) |
| `-T <type>` | Force interpretation as a specific protocol type regardless of port |

## Misc

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show usage and exit |
| `--version` | Print version and exit |
| `-f` | Print foreign (non-local) IPv4 addresses numerically |

Full manual: `man tcpdump`; filter syntax details: `man pcap-filter`.

Project.FAQ:
### `tcpdump: <iface>: You don't have permission to capture on that device`

Either run with `sudo`, or set capabilities once as shown in [Getting Started](/tcpdump/getting-started/) so your normal user can capture directly.

### Captured packets are truncated

The default snapshot length historically truncated packets to 262144 bytes in modern tcpdump (older defaults were 68 or 96 bytes and *did* commonly truncate). If you still see truncation, pass `-s 0` explicitly to capture full packets regardless of size.

### tshark reads my `.pcap` fine but some other tool rejects it

By default tcpdump writes the older `pcap` format, not `pcapng`. If a tool insists on pcapng, convert with `tshark -r in.pcap -w out.pcapng`, or capture directly with a tool that defaults to pcapng.

### `tcpdump: no suitable device found`

Run `tcpdump -D` to see what libpcap can actually find. On containers/VMs the interface may not appear until the container has `NET_RAW`/`NET_ADMIN` capabilities granted to it (e.g. `docker run --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --cap-add=NET_RAW`), or may need `--network host` to see the host's real interfaces at all.

### I don't see any packets even though traffic is flowing

Most commonly this is the switched-network issue described in [Interfaces And Privileges](/tcpdump/interfaces-and-privileges/) — you're only on the wire for your own traffic. Confirm the interface name is right (`-D`), confirm the filter isn't accidentally excluding everything (test with no filter at all first), and confirm you're not filtering on the wrong host's perspective (e.g. `src`/`dst` reversed).

### `-w` file grows huge fast

Full-payload captures on a busy interface fill disk quickly. Narrow the filter to just what you need, drop to `-s <n>` if you only need headers, or use `-C`/`-G` with `-W` (see [Rotating Captures](/tcpdump/rotating-captures/)) to cap total disk use.

### tcpdump vs tshark — which one?

tcpdump is simpler, more universally preinstalled, and better for scripting/servers. [tshark](/tshark/) understands far more protocols for deep dissection and has a friendlier display-filter language (`http.request`, `tls.handshake.type`) — reach for tshark when you need to actually read a specific protocol's fields, and tcpdump when you just need to capture or do a quick BPF-level filter.

### Capturing on loopback (`lo`)

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i lo -n 'port 5432'
```

Works the same as any other interface — useful for watching traffic between two processes on the same machine (e.g. an app talking to a local database) without it ever hitting a real NIC.

Learn by Examples.Diagnosing A Flaky Connection End-To-End:
A support ticket says "the app hangs for a few seconds every so often, then recovers." No app logs explain it. Here's a realistic tcpdump session that walks through nearly every important flag to find the cause — in this case, a slow DNS resolver being retried.

## 1. Set up so you don't need `sudo` every time

```bash
sudo setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin=eip $(command -v tcpdump)
getcap $(command -v tcpdump)
```

## 2. Find the right interface

```bash
tcpdump -D
```

```
1.eth0 [Up, Running]
2.docker0 [Up, Running]
3.any (Pseudo-device that captures on all interfaces) [Up, Running]
4.lo [Up, Running, Loopback]
```

The app runs directly on the host, so `eth0` (option 1) is the real candidate — not `docker0`, not `lo`.

## 3. Start broad, confirm traffic exists at all

```bash
tcpdump -i eth0 -c 20
```

No `sudo` needed since the capabilities are set. Twenty packets scroll by — confirms the interface is live and picking up traffic.

## 4. Narrow to the suspect: DNS

The app calls out to an API by hostname, so DNS is the first suspect. Snaplen matters here — DNS responses can be large — so it's set explicitly even though `0` is now the default, to be safe on older systems:

```bash
tcpdump -i eth0 -n -s 0 -tttt 'udp port 53'
```

- `-n` skips resolving the very addresses being looked up (that would be circular and slow)
- `-tttt` prints full timestamps so gaps are easy to eyeball
- `udp port 53` is the BPF filter for DNS

Output shows something like:

```
2026-09-27 14:02:11.001233 IP 10.0.0.7.51422 > 1.1.1.1.53: 0x9a12+ A? api.example.com. (33)
2026-09-27 14:02:14.003891 IP 10.0.0.7.51422 > 1.1.1.1.53: 0x9a12+ A? api.example.com. (33)
2026-09-27 14:02:14.041207 IP 1.1.1.1.53 > 10.0.0.7.51422: 0x9a12 1/0/0 A 203.0.113.9 (49)
```

Same query ID (`0x9a12`) sent twice, three seconds apart, before a reply finally lands — a resolver retry, which lines up exactly with the reported multi-second hang.

## 5. Capture the evidence to a file for the ticket

```bash
tcpdump -i eth0 -w dns-hang.pcap -s 0 'udp port 53' -c 200
```

`-w` saves raw packets (openable later in Wireshark or tshark); `-c 200` bounds it so it doesn't run forever unattended.

## 6. Read it back and go deeper on one exchange

```bash
tcpdump -r dns-hang.pcap -n -tttt -v
```

`-v` adds TTL/length/checksum detail on the read-back pass — worth doing once interactively even though it wasn't used during the live capture, since re-reading a file costs nothing.

## 7. Confirm it's not a duplicate-query bug in the app itself

Bare-SYN filtering isn't relevant to UDP, but the same "is this really retried at the network level" question comes up for TCP connects too. As a sanity check that the *TCP* side of the API call isn't also retrying:

```bash
tcpdump -r dns-hang.pcap -n 'tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn'
```

(Empty output here — confirming the delay really is DNS, not a TCP-level retry, and ruling out a second hypothesis in one line.)

## 8. Clean up

```bash
sudo setcap -r $(command -v tcpdump)
```

Only bother if this was a one-off diagnostic machine and you don't want the standing capability left in place.

## What this walkthrough covered

`-D`, `-i`, `-c`, `-n`, `-s`, `-tttt`, `-w`, `-r`, `-v`, BPF host/port primitives, the `tcp[tcpflags]` byte-offset trick, `setcap`/`getcap`, and the general workflow of *broad capture → narrow filter → save → re-read with more detail* that applies to almost any tcpdump investigation.
